meaning: That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain').

phonemes.desc: The dh is a voiced aspirate — “d” with breath; the a is long “ah”.
The word is the abstract noun from √dhṛ, “to hold, sustain” — that which holds the world up.

pronunciation.note: Not a god but a principle — personified as a god in the epics, whence this entry. In compounds the stem appears as dharma-; Middle Indic shortens it to dhamma-.

domains.title: That Which Holds: Law, Duty, and Righteousness
domains.subtitle: The Moral Order Personified
domains.lead: Dharma is the load-bearing word of Indian civilization: the law that holds the cosmos, the duty that holds the person, the order that holds society. From √dhṛ, ‘to sustain’, it names everything that keeps the world from sliding into chaos — and in the epics it walks as a person: the god of righteousness, father of Yudhiṣṭhira, who came down to test his own devotees.

cards.name: The Load-Bearer
cards.desc: The cosmos rests on dharma; the four feet of the bull of dharma mark the four ages of time.

cards.name: Duty by Caste and Stage
cards.desc: Svadharma — one’s own duty by birth and life-stage: the Bhagavadgītā’s central teaching.

cards.name: The Cosmic Ages
cards.desc: The four yugas are the four feet of the bull: four in the Kṛta age, one stumbling foot in ours.

cards.name: The Tester of Men
cards.desc: In the epics Dharma appears in disguise — a beggar, a dog, a crane — to test righteousness where it counts.

mythology.lead: Dharma’s mythology is the epics’ moral machinery: the god of righteousness fathers the eldest Pāṇḍava, tests his devotees in disguise, and — in the Nala story — teaches dice to a king as the instrument of ruin. He has no cult-image because he is what every cult-image stands for; yet the tradition gave him a family and a biography.

myths.title: The Father of Yudhiṣṭhira
myths.text: When Pāṇḍu was cursed to die on his wedding night, his queens invoked the gods: Dharmarāja himself, the god of righteousness, fathered Yudhiṣṭhira on Kuntī. The eldest Pāṇḍava is thus dharma’s son — which is why the epic keeps asking whether righteousness itself can survive the dice-game and the war it forces.

myths.title: The Tests in Disguise
myths.text: The epic’s forest-books stage Dharma’s examinations: as a stork demanding why Yudhiṣṭhira would not abandon a fallen brother; as a Yakṣa whose riddles the king answers with the epic’s most quoted verses; as a dog who follows the Pāṇḍavas to heaven’s gate and is refused entry — until Yudhiṣṭhira refuses heaven without it. The dog was Dharma; the gate opens.

myths.title: The God Who Taught Dice
myths.text: In the Nala episode, Kali — the demon of the Kali Yuga — begs Dharma for a means to enter the righteous king Nala; Dharma, inexplicably, teaches him dice. The story’s commentators wrestled for centuries with the god of righteousness arming the demon of strife: the standard resolution — even dharma’s permission is a test that righteousness must survive.

myths.title: The Son of Brahmā
myths.text: The Purāṇas give Dharma genealogy: born of Brahmā’s breast as one of the mind-born sons, husband of Dhṛti and father of the personified virtues — Kāma (desire), Lobha (greed), Darpa (pride) and the rest. The abstraction’s family-tree is the Indian psyche’s map of its own forces.

lore.syncretism: Dharma and the Buddha’s Dhamma share a word and a mission: the Buddha claimed the title Dharmarāja, king of the law, and made dharma’s wheel — the dharmacakra — his teaching’s emblem. The Zoroastrian daēnā and the Roman Fas are the comparison-points scholars cite; in India itself dharma absorbed every local law-code, from the Vedic ṛta to the medieval digests.
lore.culturalLegacy: The word is untranslatable and indispensable — every rendering (‘law’, ‘duty’, ‘religion’, ‘righteousness’) is a fraction. The four feet of dharma’s bull are India’s theory of history; the Bhagavadgītā’s ‘better one’s own dharma, though defective’ is among the most quoted ethical sentences on earth. India’s modern name for itself, ‘Hindu Dharma’, keeps the word at the nation’s centre.
lore.extendedMeditation: Dharma: the name of the thing that holds, restored in letters that hold nothing but carry everything. It needs no mark over its vowels — the word’s burden is its own diacritic, the weight of the worlds it has held for four thousand years.

sources.name: Purāṇic genealogies of the mind-born sons

lore.archaeology: Dharma’s monuments are juridical: the edict-pillars of Aśoka, whose dhamma inscriptions are the oldest deciphered moral legislation on earth. His wheel crowns the Indian flag; his bull — the dharmavṛṣabha — kneels on the seal of the Republic.
lore.cult: No temple of Dharma stands alone, yet every temple is his: he is worshipped as Yudhiṣṭhira’s father and as the law itself at the Dharmaśāstra recitations. The Kurukshetra pilgrim circuit treats the epic’s battlefield as his sanctum.
lore.iconography: Rarely imaged; when personified, a grave king with the plough or the wheel, often with Yudhiṣṭhira beside him. His true icon is the bull’s four legs, the wheel’s eight spokes, the scales of the king’s court — the law’s geometry rather than its face.
lore.reception: Comparative law and religion use dharma as the test-case of an untranslatable that must be translated anyway; sociology of religion treats it as the most successful fusion of cosmic, social, and personal order ever devised. ‘Dharma’ entered English dictionaries as a loan-word — the surest sign a civilization’s key term refused to be carried.
